claims.claim: A Viking base / longphort is reported as re-established at Waterford in AD914 after an interruption around AD902.
Hiberno-Norse Waterford occupied triangular ground bounded by the River Suir and marshy ground around St John's River, with the eastern apex in the later Reginald's Tower area.
The 10th-century settlement is interpreted as centred on the eastern end of the promontory around Dundory.
Two large roughly north-south ditches were excavated at Bailey's New Street in 1999.
The Bailey's New Street ditches are interpreted as likely related to defences east of the excavation and may mark a Dundory western limit.
The form, date and size of Waterford's earliest quayside remain poorly known; a measured Viking quay line is not currently defensible.
Arundel Square preserves late-Viking urban evidence including 11th-century structures, a paved Peter Street surface, three-aisled houses, smaller rear structures, paths and property boundaries.
High Street is described in published excavation reporting as one of Waterford's principal late-Viking streets.
A timber from a Peter Street / Olaf Street sunken-featured structure was reported with a date around AD1083, making it a post-1050 chronological control.
Bakehouse Lane Viking town defences included a large ditch and inner bank; ditch timbers produced dendrochronological dates centred on AD1070–1080.
Masonry encountered in 2013 at Bailey's New Street was initially considered possible town wall but subsequent monitoring indicated it may instead be a road surface.
